Agree a two-minute review with two questions only: what actually happened, and what would a kind observer say. Then a physical switch. Practice on the last event the client replayed.

fields.label: The event I keep replaying
What I replay most (a sentence, a look, a pause)
My two-minute review: what actually happened
What a kind observer would say
My switch when the two minutes are up
How long the replay used to last, and how long it lasted this time

title: Social Prediction Log
summary: Records the client's forecast before a social situation and the outcome after, to compare over weeks.
goal: Build the client's own evidence that their predictions run far worse than events.
body_md: The forecast must be specific and rated: they will notice me blushing and think less of me, seventy percent. Afterward the client records what observably happened, not how it felt. Review the gap across ten entries, which is usually where belief shifts rather than in any single event.

fields.label: The upcoming situation
What I predict will happen, specifically
How sure I am (0-100%)
What observably happened
How I know (what people said or did)
How the prediction compared
What I predict next time, adjusted

title: Conversation Toolkit Card
summary: A pocket card of openers, follow-up questions and graceful exits for social situations.
goal: Reduce the load of inventing conversation so the client can practice being in it.
body_md: Build it with the client's own words, not scripts from a book, and include exits, since knowing they can leave makes staying easier. Warn against using it as a safety behavior: the card is for learning, and the goal is to need it less. Rehearse a full opener-question-exit in session.

fields.label: Three openers I could actually say
Three follow-up questions that work in most conversations
Two ways to leave a conversation gracefully
What I will do with my hands
The one I will try first this week
How it went, and whether I needed the card

title: Social Brave Steps for Teens
summary: A teen's own ladder of social situations from easy to hard, with a brave step per week.
goal: Give a teenager a graded, self-chosen path back into the social situations they have been dodging.
body_md: Let the teen build and order the steps; a ladder chosen by an adult will not be climbed. Keep parents to a support role agreed on the sheet. Steps should be specific: ask one question in class, not participate more. Celebrate attempts, not outcomes, and expect a step to be repeated before moving up.

fields.label: Situations I have been avoiding
My ladder, easiest at the bottom
This week's step
What I am afraid will happen
What actually happened
What my parent will do (and not do) to help
The step for next week

title: Continuing Bonds Letter
summary: A letter to the person who died, about what has happened since and what the client still carries of them.
goal: Support an ongoing connection with the person rather than a closing of the door.
body_md: Offer it as one option among several, since some clients find writing to the dead unbearable and others find it the only thing that helps. Frame the bond as something that changes rather than ends. The client decides whether to read it aloud, keep it, or take it somewhere. Include 988 among the prompts for the darkest hours.

fields.label: What I want to tell you about since you died
What I have kept of you (a habit, a phrase, an object, a way of seeing)
What I wish I had said
What I think you would say to me now
How I will keep you in my life going forward
If the grief ever gets dangerously dark: 988 (call or text), and who else I will reach

title: Grief Triggers Calendar
summary: A year at a glance with the dates, seasons and events likely to bring the grief up hard.
goal: Let the client see the hard days coming and plan support for them instead of being ambushed.
body_md: Include the obvious dates and the sideways ones: the first snow, the tax season the person used to handle, the song at the store. Plan for the week before an anniversary, which is often worse than the day. Decide with the client who will know about each date.

fields.label: Anniversaries and birthdays
Seasons, holidays and rituals that will be different
Sideways reminders I can predict
The next hard date, and what I will do that day
Who will know it is coming
What helped on the last hard date, and what did not

title: Dual Process Week Planner
summary: A week planned with time for facing the loss and time for the ordinary business of living, both on purpose.
goal: Normalize moving between grief and daily life instead of feeling guilty about either.
body_md: Explain that healthy grief moves between the loss and the rest of life, and that neither side is avoidance. Clients stuck on one side feel guilty when they laugh, or numb when they cannot cry; the planner gives both permission. Keep the entries small and concrete.

fields.label: Times this week I will let myself be with the loss (looking at photos, visiting, talking about them)
Times this week I will do ordinary or even pleasant things
The side I tend to get stuck on
What guilt says when I switch sides
What I will say back to it
How the week went

title: Memory Box Project
summary: A child decorates a box and fills it with objects, drawings and stories that hold the person who died.
goal: Give a grieving child a concrete, permitted place for their memories and a way to talk about them.
body_md: Let the child lead on what goes in and what stays private. Each item comes with a story the child tells if they want to; the telling is the work. Involve the surviving parent or carer where possible, and coach them to follow the child's pace rather than their own. Revisit the box on hard dates.

fields.label: What my box looks like
The first three things I put in it, and why
A story that goes with one of them
Something I want to ask about the person who died
Who I can open the box with
When I might want to open it

title: Grief Conversation Cards
summary: A deck of gentle prompts about the person who died, drawn in turn by family members or a group.
goal: Let a family or group talk about the person in a structured, low-pressure way.
body_md: Write the prompts with the group first so nothing on a card ambushes anyone, mixing light ones with heavier ones. Any card can be passed. Play in a circle with a talking object. In families, children often answer more freely than adults, which gives the adults permission.

fields.label: Prompts we put on the cards
The card I drew, and what I said
Something I learned about the person from someone else
A card I passed on
The card I would like to answer next time

title: Needs Inventory for Partners
summary: Each partner lists their needs in the relationship, ranked, and guesses their partner's list before comparing.
goal: Replace assumed needs with stated ones, and show each partner what the other has been guessing.
body_md: Have both partners complete it separately, including the guess about each other, before any discussion. The gaps between the guess and the real list are the material. Keep the tone of curiosity when a partner's need surprises the other; surprise is information, not an accusation.

fields.label: My top five needs in this relationship, ranked
How well each is being met right now (0-10)
What I think my partner's top five are
What surprised me about their real list
One need of theirs I could meet better this month
One need of mine I will ask for directly

title: Perpetual Problems Sorter
summary: Sorts a couple's recurring arguments into the solvable and the perpetual, and plans a different approach to each.
goal: Stop a couple from trying to solve what needs managing, and from managing what could be solved.
body_md: List the arguments first, then sort. Perpetual problems come from differences in personality or values and will be there in ten years; the goal is dialogue and humor about them, not a fix. Solvable problems get a concrete plan. Most couples are relieved to hear that having perpetual problems is normal.

fields.label: Arguments we have more than once a month
Which of these come from a difference in who we are
Which could actually be solved with a plan
For one solvable problem: our plan
For one perpetual problem: what we can each accept
How we will talk about the perpetual one next time it comes up

title: Trust Rebuilding Steps
summary: A shared ladder of specific, observable actions that would rebuild trust after a breach, with a timeline.
goal: Turn a vague demand to earn trust back into steps both partners can see happening.
body_md: The hurt partner names what would help; the other partner says what they can commit to. Steps must be observable, since promises to change are not. Agree how long the checking phase lasts, because trust cannot rebuild under permanent surveillance. Review progress monthly in session.

fields.label: What was broken, in one sentence each
Actions that would help me trust again (specific and visible)
Which of these I can commit to, and when
What transparency looks like for now, and for how long
What I need to hear when I have a wobble
How we will mark progress

title: Communication Pattern Replay
summary: Replays one recent exchange line by line, with each partner naming what they meant and what they heard.
goal: Show a couple the gap between what was said, what was meant and what landed.
body_md: Pick a short exchange, not the biggest fight. Write the actual lines, then have each partner add what they meant and what they heard. The gaps are usually where the fight lives. Finish by rewriting two lines each, and rehearse the rewrite in session.

fields.label: The exchange, line by line, as it happened
For my lines: what I meant
For their lines: what I heard
Where the gap between meant and heard was widest
Two lines I would rewrite
How the rewritten version sounds out loud

title: Relationship Values Compass
summary: Each partner names the kind of partner they want to be, separately from how the other is behaving.
goal: Anchor each partner to their own values so change does not wait on the other person moving first.
body_md: Works with a couple or with one partner alone. The key move is separating my values as a partner from what I get back; clients often discover they have been acting on a scoreboard. Choose one valued action for the week that does not depend on the other person's response.

fields.label: The partner I want to be, in three words
How I have actually been acting lately
What I have been waiting for my partner to do first
One valued action I will take this week regardless
What my mind says will happen if I go first
What actually happened

title: Safety and Stabilization Plan
summary: A plan for the practical and emotional safety a survivor needs in place before any deeper work.
goal: Put steady ground under the client first: who, where, what, and what to do when it gets too much.
body_md: Complete it together in session and never as homework. Cover present-day safety from the person who harmed them, the people who help, the skills that bring them back, and what to do in the worst hours. Move at the client's pace and do not ask for the details of what happened; that is not what this sheet is for. Include 988.

fields.label: Am I safe from the person now? What would make me safer
People I trust, and what each one can help with
Skills that bring me back when I am flooded
Signs that I am doing too much too fast
What I will do in the worst hour: 988 (call or text), and my other numbers
What I want my therapist to know about pace
What I am not ready to talk about yet, and that is fine

title: Consent and Boundaries Map
summary: Maps the client's yes, no and maybe across touch, closeness and conversation, in their own words.
goal: Help a survivor reclaim the right to decide, in small everyday ways, what they allow and what they do not.
body_md: Keep it to everyday boundaries at first: hugs, sitting close, questions from family, who has their number. The maybe column matters, since survivors often feel boundaries must be absolute to count. Rehearse one no in session. Nothing here asks about the abuse itself.

fields.label: Things I am a clear yes to
Things I am a clear no to
Things that are a maybe, and what would make them a yes
A boundary someone in my life keeps crossing
How I will say no to that, in my words
What I will do if they push
Someone who respects my boundaries well

title: Shame Response Sheet
summary: Catches the self-blame that follows abuse, tests it against what the client would say to another survivor, and writes the fairer version.
goal: Loosen the belief that the client caused, allowed or deserved what happened.
body_md: Do this in session, gently, and expect the double standard to be stark: the client will extend to another survivor a compassion they refuse themselves. Do not argue the client out of the belief; let the comparison do the work, and rate belief before and after. Stop if the client becomes flooded and return to grounding.

fields.label: What I tell myself about why it happened
How much I believe that (0-100%)
What I would say to a friend who told me the same story
Where the blame actually belongs
The fairer statement, in my words
How much I believe the fairer statement now (0-100%)

title: Support Disclosure Planner
summary: Plans whether, who, when and how much to tell, so a disclosure happens on the client's terms.
goal: Keep the choice of who knows, and how much, in the survivor's hands.
body_md: Not telling is a valid outcome of this sheet and should be said out loud. Work through what the client wants from telling, who is likely to respond well, and how much to say; a first sentence and an exit line are worth rehearsing. Plan for the reaction being disappointing, since it sometimes is.

fields.label: What I hope telling someone would give me
People I might tell, and how I think each would respond
The person I would tell first, if anyone
How much I want to say (a sentence is enough)
My first sentence
How I will end the conversation if I need to
What I will do for myself afterward, whatever their reaction

title: Body Safety Rules Poster
summary: A child makes a poster of body safety rules: private parts, okay and not-okay touch, secrets versus surprises, and who to tell.
goal: Teach a child the words and the permission to tell, as part of prevention work with families.
body_md: A prevention and education tool, done with a parent in the room where possible. Use correct names for body parts. Teach that surprises are fun and short and secrets about bodies are never kept. List five trusted adults. If a child discloses during this, stop the activity, stay calm, believe them, and follow your mandated reporting duties.

fields.label: Private parts have proper names, and mine are
Okay touch and not-okay touch: my examples
The difference between a surprise and a secret
My five trusted grown-ups
What I say if someone breaks a body safety rule
Where my poster will hang

title: Coping Menu by Situation
summary: A menu of the client's coping options sorted by where they are: at work, in public, at home, in bed.
goal: Match skills to settings so the right one is available where the distress actually happens.
body_md: Most clients have skills that only work at home and distress that happens elsewhere. Sort by setting and check that each setting has at least two options that are invisible to other people. Include one for the middle of the night. Keep the menu in the phone's notes.

fields.label: At work or school: two things I can do without anyone noticing
In public: two options
At home: two options
In bed at 3 a.m.: two options
The skill I reach for too often, and where it does not work
The new skill I will try this week, and where

title: Skill Practice Log
summary: A weekly log of which coping skill the client used, in what situation, and how well it worked.
goal: Turn coping from a vague resolve into a tracked practice with results.
body_md: The rating is the useful part: a skill that scores three out of ten in three different situations can be retired without guilt. Look for the mismatch between skills tried and situations faced. Praise the attempt, especially when the skill did not work, since trying is what builds the habit.

fields.label: Date and the situation
Distress before (0-10)
The skill I used
Distress after (0-10)
How well it worked (0-10) and why
A skill I could have used instead
The skill I will practice most next week

title: Coping Ladder for Kids
summary: A ladder of a child's coping moves from small feelings at the bottom to big ones at the top.
goal: Match the size of the coping move to the size of the feeling, in a picture a child can use.
body_md: Draw a ladder with three or four rungs and let the child assign feelings sizes to each. Small feelings get small moves: a breath, a drink of water. Big feelings get big moves: a break, a grown-up. Practice one move per rung in session and have the parent post the ladder at home.

fields.label: Bottom rung: a small feeling and my small move
Middle rung: a medium feeling and my medium move
Top rung: a huge feeling and my biggest move
How I know which rung I am on
Who helps me on the top rung
Where my ladder is posted

title: Coping Skills Relay
summary: Teams race to act out or demonstrate a coping skill for each situation card drawn.
goal: Rehearse coping skills under mild pressure and laughter, so they are practiced rather than just known.
body_md: Write situation cards with the group beforehand: a test tomorrow, a friend ignoring a text, a loud house. A team scores when the skill fits the situation and could actually be done there. Judge fit, not speed, and let the group argue the call; the argument is the learning.

fields.label: Situation cards we made
Skills my team demonstrated
A skill another team showed that I want to steal
A situation none of us could match well
The skill I will practice this week

title: Helpful vs Costly Coping Sort
summary: Sorts everything the client does to feel better into what helps in the long run and what costs more than it gives.
goal: Help the client judge coping by its long-term workability rather than by how fast it works.
body_md: List everything without judgment first, including the ones the client is ashamed of; those are usually the fastest-acting. Sort by long-term workability, not by how they look. Most clients find a few things belong in both columns depending on amount, which is worth writing down rather than resolving.

fields.label: Everything I do to feel better, fast or slow
Which ones help me next week too
Which ones cost more than they give
Which ones depend on how much
One costly one I will shrink, and how
One helpful one I will do more of, and when

title: Phobia Prediction Tracker
summary: Records what the client expects to happen around the feared object or situation and what actually occurs.
goal: Build the client's own evidence that the feared outcome and the felt danger diverge.
body_md: Ask for the specific feared outcome, not just fear: I will faint, the dog will bite, the plane will crash. Rate belief before and after each approach. The pattern across entries is what changes belief, so aim for at least eight entries before drawing conclusions together.

fields.label: The feared thing and the situation
What I predict will happen, specifically
How sure I am (0-100%)
Peak fear (0-10)
What actually happened
What I did during the peak
My belief in the prediction now (0-100%)

title: Approach Steps Planner
summary: Plans the next approach step toward a feared object in detail: where, how long, with whom, and what to drop.
goal: Make each approach step concrete enough to actually happen this week.
body_md: One step at a time, planned to the minute. Include what safety moves the client will drop, since carrying the escape plan into the step blunts it. Decide in advance how long to stay: long enough for the fear to fall, not just to touch and run. Debrief in session before planning the next.

fields.label: This week's step
Where and when, exactly
Who will be there, and what they will and will not do
How long I will stay (until fear drops by half)
The safety moves I will not use
What happened, and what I will do next week

title: Phobia Body Response Sheet
summary: Names what the client's body does around the feared thing, and separates the alarm from the danger.
goal: Help the client see the fear response as an alarm that can fire without a fire.
body_md: Map the response: heart, breath, muscles, stomach, the urge to run. Explain plainly that the body's alarm is doing its job and that the job is to get them out, which is why staying feels wrong. For blood or needle fears, note the faint response and plan applied tension separately.

fields.label: What my body does first around the feared thing
What it does next
The urge that comes with it
What the alarm is trying to make me do
What I know about the real danger in this situation
What I will do with the alarm next time it fires

title: Brave Practice Chart for Kids
summary: A sticker chart for a child's repeated brave practices with a feared thing, tied to a small reward.
goal: Make repetition of approach steps visible and rewarding for a child.
duration: 20 minutes to set up, then daily
body_md: Choose practices small enough to repeat daily: look at a picture of a dog, stand in the doorway with the lights off. Stickers go on for attempts, not for calm. Parents hold the chart and the reward and keep their own anxiety out of the practice. Change the practice when it stops earning fear.

fields.label: My brave practice this week
Stickers I earned
How scared I was the first time (0-10) and the last time
My reward when the chart is full
What my grown-up does during practice
Next week's brave practice

title: Fear Ladder Card Sort
summary: Situations written on cards and physically sorted into a ladder from least to most scary.
goal: Build a fear hierarchy as a hands-on sorting task rather than a form.
body_md: Write one situation per card with the client, at least fifteen, then sort them on the table or floor. The physical sorting draws out distinctions a form misses, and the client can move cards as beliefs change. Photograph the finished ladder and use it to choose the next approach step.

fields.label: Situations we wrote on cards
The bottom three cards
The top three cards
Cards I moved while sorting, and why
The card I will start with
The card I cannot imagine reaching yet

title: Body Neutrality Practice
summary: Daily short statements about what the body did today rather than how it looked.
goal: Move the client's relationship with their body from judgment toward function and use.
duration: Two minutes daily for two weeks
body_md: Aim for neutral, not positive; clients who cannot believe their body is beautiful can believe it carried them up the stairs. Keep the statements about doing and feeling. Notice when the client sneaks an appearance comment in and gently redirect. Never mention weight, shape or food in this practice.

fields.label: Three things my body did for me today
One thing it let me feel (warmth, music, a hug, the wind)
A neutral statement about my body, without judgment either way
What my mind wanted to add about how it looks
How I responded to that
The statement I will use tomorrow morning

title: Body Checking Log
summary: Records the mirror checks, pinching, comparing and photo scrutiny that keep body worry alive, and what each one did to mood.
goal: Show the client how checking feeds the worry, and plan a reduction.
body_md: Checking feels like getting information but produces worse mood almost every time; the log makes that visible. Include the quiet forms: reflections in windows, comparing in group photos, clothes tried and discarded. Plan one check to cut in half, not to stop entirely.

fields.label: Date and time
What I checked, and how (mirror, pinch, photo, comparing)
What I was looking for
Mood before and after (0-10)
How long the reassurance lasted, if any
The check I will cut in half next week
What I will do instead in that moment

title: Appearance Assumptions Sheet
summary: Lists the client's rules linking appearance to worth, acceptance or success, and tests each one.
goal: Loosen the beliefs that make appearance carry the whole weight of self-worth.
body_md: Draw out the if-then rules: if I looked different, then people would... Test each against the client's own experience and the people they admire. The goal is to shrink the share of self-worth that appearance holds, which a pie chart of what makes up their worth can show before and after.

fields.label: My rules about appearance (if I looked..., then...)
Where each rule came from
Evidence from my own life for and against it
People I admire, and how much their looks have to do with it
How much of my self-worth appearance holds now (%)
What else I would like it to rest on

title: Body Gratitude Function List
summary: A list of what the client's body has carried them through, by life stage, written as a record rather than a rating.
goal: Build a history of the body as a companion rather than an object under review.
body_md: Move through life stages: childhood play, illness survived, work done, people carried, places reached. The tone is a record, not a pep talk. Clients with a history of harming or overworking their body may find this tender; slow down there. No comments on shape or size anywhere on the sheet.

fields.label: What my body did for me as a child
What it has carried me through
What it lets me do that I would miss
Someone it has held or helped
Something it recovered from
What I would like to thank it for, plainly

title: Media Diet Audit
summary: An inventory of the accounts, shows and images the client consumes, and what each does to how they feel in their body.
goal: Change what the client feeds their body image, since much of it arrives through a screen.
body_md: Go through the phone together. For each account or habit, ask what it does to the client's body feeling in the ten minutes after. Unfollowing is a real intervention and often the fastest one; replace, do not just remove, so the feed is not empty. Repeat in a month.

fields.label: Accounts and shows I see most
How I feel in my body after each (better, worse, nothing)
The ones that leave me comparing
Accounts I will unfollow or mute this week
What I will follow instead (bodies doing things, other interests entirely)
How my feed feels after the change

title: Energy Budget Planner
summary: A weekly map of what fills a client’s energy and what drains it, sorted by cost and value.
goal: Help the client spend limited energy on what actually matters to them.
body_md: Have the client list the week’s activities and sort each into drains and refills, then rate the cost of each drain against how much they chose it versus felt obligated to it. The pattern that usually surfaces is a client spending most of their budget on obligation with little left for anything restorative. Use it to plan one small swap for the coming week, not a full overhaul.

fields.label: Activities that drain my energy this week
Activities that refill my energy this week
Drains I chose versus drains I felt stuck with
One drain I could trim or hand off
One refill I could add, even briefly

title: Daily Values Check-In
summary: A short end-of-day rating of how closely today’s actions matched what the client cares about.
goal: Build the client’s habit of noticing values in action, not just in theory.
duration: Five minutes daily for two weeks
body_md: The client picks two or three values to track and rates, each evening, how much today’s choices lined up with each one. This works best paired with a values list from an earlier session rather than started cold. Look together at the low-rated days for what got in the way, and the high-rated days for what made room.

fields.label: The values I am tracking this week
Today’s rating for each, and why
What got in the way today
What made room today

title: Weekly Wins Log
summary: A running list of small things the client did well this week, sized so they actually get written down.
goal: Counter a habit of noticing only what went wrong.
body_md: Set the bar low from the start: a win can be as small as answering an email or getting out of bed on time. Clients who discount their own effort will need the clinician to model this the first few entries. Read the week back together in session rather than leaving it as homework the client reviews alone.

fields.label: Monday
Tuesday
Wednesday
Thursday
Friday
Saturday and Sunday
The win I am most surprised I almost skipped

title: Assertive Request Builder
summary: A script-building sheet that turns a vague complaint into a specific, askable request.
goal: Give the client a repeatable structure for asking for what they need.
body_md: Start from a real situation the client is avoiding and walk the sheet’s sequence: the observation, the feeling, the specific request, and the reason it matters. Clients often draft an accusation first; the work is trimming it down to a request the other person could actually say yes to. Rehearse the final line out loud before the client leaves.

fields.label: What happened, in neutral, factual terms
How it affected me
What I want to ask for, specifically
Why this matters to me
My one-sentence request, written out to practice

title: Comfort Zone Expansion Map
summary: A ring diagram sorting activities the client already does, avoids, and might try next.
goal: Give the client a visual, low-pressure ladder toward things they have been avoiding.
body_md: Draw three rings: comfortable, stretching, and out of reach for now. Sort a list of activities the client names into the rings together, then pick one item from the stretch ring to try before the next session. Keep the outer ring visible but untouched; it is there to show growth, not to pressure a leap.

fields.label: What I already do comfortably
What feels like a stretch but possible
What feels out of reach for now
The one stretch item I will try this week
What would make that item easier to attempt

title: Thinking Trap Field Guide
summary: A pocket reference of common thinking traps with the client’s own examples next to each.
goal: Help the client recognize a thinking trap by its shape, not just its name.
body_md: Introduce each trap with a plain description and let the client supply a recent example of their own rather than a textbook one; a self-generated example is far easier to spot next time. Add to the guide over several sessions instead of filling it in one sitting. The finished sheet works as a quick-reference the client can reread before a hard conversation.

fields.label: All-or-nothing thinking: my example
Mind reading: my example
Fortune telling: my example
Catastrophizing: my example
Should statements: my example
The trap I fall into most often

title: Behavioral Experiment Design Sheet
summary: A step-by-step sheet for testing a feared prediction against what actually happens.
goal: Replace a client’s assumption with their own evidence.
duration: 20 minutes to plan, then the week to run it
body_md: The sheet earns its keep in the prediction line: get a specific, falsifiable guess before the client runs the experiment, not a vague sense of dread. Plan the smallest version that still tests the belief, and agree in session on what would count as disconfirming evidence so the client cannot explain it away afterward. Debrief the result together at the next appointment.

fields.label: The belief I am testing
My specific prediction of what will happen
How confident I am in that prediction (0-100)
The experiment I will run
What actually happened
What this tells me about the original belief

title: Core Belief Ladder
summary: A worksheet that climbs from one automatic thought up to the core belief underneath it.
goal: Help the client see the deeper rule driving a repeated reaction.
body_md: Start with a fresh automatic thought and ask, at each rung, what it would mean if it were true, climbing toward the underlying rule about the self, others, or the world. This can land somewhere raw, so pace it and stay with the client’s reaction rather than rushing to the top rung. Once named, the belief becomes something to track and gently test rather than argue with directly.

fields.label: The automatic thought I am starting from
If that were true, what would it mean about me?
And if that were true, what would it mean?
The core belief I landed on
Where I first remember believing this

title: Activity and Mood Bridge
summary: A same-day log pairing what the client did with how their mood shifted afterward.
goal: Show the client the link between activity and mood before asking them to change either.
body_md: Log activities and a mood rating before and after, without judging the activity as good or bad in advance; the point is to let the data show which activities lift mood and which ones flatten it, since it is often not what the client expects. Review the pattern together rather than telling the client the answer, and use it to choose next week’s activities deliberately.

fields.label: Time and activity
Mood before (0-10)
Mood after (0-10)
Anything unexpected about the shift
The activity that moved my mood most this week

title: Balanced Thought Builder
summary: A three-column sheet that turns one automatic thought into a more balanced alternative.
goal: Give the client a repeatable way to talk back to an automatic thought.
body_md: The middle column is where the work happens: evidence for and against the automatic thought, gathered without letting either side be skipped. A balanced thought is not a forced positive; it should sound like something the client could actually believe, even a little skeptically. Practice saying the balanced thought out loud, since it lands differently than reading it silently.

fields.label: The automatic thought
Evidence that supports it
Evidence against it
A more balanced thought
How much I believe the balanced thought (0-100)

title: Anchor in the Present Practice
summary: A short breath-and-senses script the client rehearses in session, then uses before hard moments.
goal: Give the client a fast way to drop out of their head and into the room.
body_md: Walk the three steps in session first: a few slow breaths, naming what can be sensed right now, and expanding attention outward to the room. Practicing it calm builds the habit before the client needs it activated. Encourage short, frequent use rather than saving it only for crisis moments, so it becomes familiar rather than a last resort.

fields.label: Where I practiced this today
What I noticed in my breath
What I noticed in the room around me
How my attention felt before versus after

title: Self-as-Sky Practice
summary: A metaphor exercise where the client practices noticing thoughts and moods as weather passing through a sky that stays the sky.
goal: Give the client a felt sense of the part of them that observes, apart from any one thought or mood.
body_md: Read the metaphor slowly and let the client sit with it rather than explaining it away: whatever weather passes through, the sky is not the storm and is not damaged by it. Afterward, ask what moods or thoughts have felt like weather this week and which ones the client had been mistaking for the sky itself. This is a practice to return to, not a one-time insight.

fields.label: The weather (thought or mood) that has been loudest this week
What changed when I pictured it as weather passing through
What stayed the same underneath the weather
Where I could use this metaphor next

title: Workability Compass
summary: A worksheet that sorts a client’s coping habits by whether they work in the long run, not just the moment.
goal: Shift the question from whether a habit feels good to whether it moves the client toward their life.
body_md: List the client’s go-to coping habits and rate each on short-term relief against long-term direction, without labeling any habit as simply good or bad. Many habits will score high on relief and low on direction, which is the useful tension to sit with rather than resolve immediately. Use the compass to choose one small experiment with a different response this week.

fields.label: A habit I use to cope
How much relief it gives right now (0-10)
How much it moves me toward the life I want (0-10)
What I notice about the gap between those two numbers
One small experiment I could try instead

title: Values Direction Step Ladder
summary: A ladder of small, values-linked steps between where the client is now and a valued direction.
goal: Turn a values conversation into a specific next step the client can actually take.
body_md: Name the value first, then work backward from the bigger picture to a first rung small enough to attempt this week. The ladder should stay visible across sessions so progress and stalls both show up honestly. When a rung gets skipped, treat it as information about the size of the step, not a failure to revisit.

fields.label: The value this ladder serves
The bigger step I am building toward
The first rung: a step small enough to try this week
What might get in the way
How I will know I took the step

title: Defusion Phrase Practice
summary: A drill for rehearsing short defusion phrases until they come to mind on their own.
goal: Build the client’s reflex to put distance between themselves and a sticky thought.
body_md: Pick two or three phrases in session, like naming a thought as "just a thought" or adding "I notice I am having the thought that" before it, and rehearse them out loud with a real example. The drill works because repetition builds the habit; a single explanation rarely sticks on its own. Track which phrase actually created distance, since not every phrase lands the same for every client.

fields.label: The sticky thought I practiced with
The defusion phrase I used
How the thought felt before
How it felt after using the phrase

title: Opposite Action Practice Card
summary: A pocket card walking through opposite action for whichever emotion is driving an unhelpful urge.
goal: Give the client a repeatable structure for acting opposite to an emotion urge that does not fit the facts.
duration: 15 minutes to learn, then in the moment
body_md: Walk through one recent example in session: name the emotion, the urge it brings, whether the urge fits the facts of the situation, and what the opposite action would look like. Opposite action works best done fully and with body language included, not halfway. Practice a small version before the client needs it for something that matters more.

fields.label: The emotion I am feeling
The urge that comes with it
Does the urge fit the facts of the situation?
The opposite action, done all the way
What happened when I tried it

title: TIPP Cool-Down Card
summary: A wallet card of the four TIPP steps for bringing a high-intensity moment down fast.
goal: Give the client a physiology-first option for a moment too intense for talking through.
body_md: Practice each TIPP option in session so the client has already felt the effect before they need it: cold water on the face, brief intense exercise, paced breathing, and paired muscle relaxation. These work on the body directly and are meant for the top of the intensity scale, not routine stress. Ask the client which option their body responded to fastest and star it on the card.

fields.label: Temperature: what I will use (cold water, ice)
Intense exercise: what I will do for one minute
Paced breathing: my count in and out
Paired muscle relaxation: which muscles I will tense and release
The option that worked fastest for me

title: Wise Mind Reflection Log
summary: A short daily log sorting a decision into emotion mind, reasonable mind, or wise mind.
goal: Build the client’s ability to notice which mind a decision is coming from before acting on it.
duration: Five minutes daily for two weeks
body_md: Describe the three minds plainly before the client starts: emotion mind runs hot, reasonable mind runs cold, and wise mind holds both. Ask the client to log one decision a day and name which mind it came from, without judging emotion mind as wrong. Over the log’s two weeks, look together for what tips a decision toward wise mind.

fields.label: The decision I made today

What reasonable mind was saying
What wise mind would add

title: Emotion Vocabulary Wheel
summary: A wheel of emotion words sorted from broad to specific for a client who tends to say only "bad" or "fine".
goal: Expand the client’s emotion vocabulary so they can name what they feel more precisely.
body_md: Start from a broad word the client already uses and work outward to more specific words on the wheel, checking which ones actually fit rather than assigning them. Naming an emotion precisely is itself a regulation skill; "bad" leaves nowhere to go, while "disappointed" or "on edge" points toward what might help. Keep the wheel on hand for a few sessions until specific words start coming more naturally.

fields.label: The broad word I usually reach for

title: DEAR MAN Rehearsal Card
summary: A script card for rehearsing a DEAR MAN request out loud before a real conversation.
goal: Get the client comfortable with the words before they need them under pressure.
body_md: Write out each DEAR MAN line for one upcoming conversation, then have the client say it out loud in session at least twice, adjusting the wording until it sounds like them. Rehearsal matters more than the sheet itself; a script read for the first time in the real conversation rarely comes out right. Note where the client’s voice or posture shifts, since that is often where the real work is.

fields.label: Describe: the facts of the situation
Express: how I feel about it
Assert: what I am asking for
Reinforce: why saying yes helps them too
What I noticed rehearsing this out loud

title: Bid for Connection Tracker
summary: A week-long log where each partner notes bids for connection they made and how the other responded.
goal: Help a couple see how often small bids happen and how they tend to answer them.
duration: One week, then a 20-minute session review
body_md: Explain a bid as any small reach for attention, affection, or support, from a comment about the weather to a hand on a shoulder. Each partner tracks their own bids and, separately, notices how they responded to the other’s. Most couples are surprised by how many bids happen daily and how easy a few are to miss; the review is where the noticing becomes useful.

fields.label: A bid I made this week
How my partner responded

title: Repair Phrase Toolkit
summary: A shared list of phrases each partner picks in advance to slow down or repair a conflict in the moment.
goal: Give a couple ready-made language for the moment a conversation starts to go badly.
body_md: Have each partner draft a few phrases that feel natural to them, such as asking for a pause or naming that things are getting heated, and read them aloud to each other in session. A phrase rehearsed together lands very differently mid-argument than one invented on the spot. Agree together on a signal for when either partner wants to use one.

title: Gratitude Exchange Cards
summary: A set of cards each partner fills out naming something specific they appreciated about the other that week.
goal: Build a couple’s habit of naming appreciation out loud rather than assuming it is known.
body_md: Ask for something specific rather than general, like a moment or action rather than a trait, so the exchange does not flatten into routine compliments. Read the cards aloud to each other rather than just handing them over; hearing it said matters. Keep a small stack of past cards, since couples often return to reread them during harder weeks.

fields.label: Partner A: something specific I appreciated this week
Partner B: something specific I appreciated this week

title: Chore Fairness Map
summary: A worksheet where each partner separately lists household tasks and who does them, before comparing notes.
goal: Surface a mismatch between each partner’s sense of who does what.
body_md: Have each partner fill out their list separately before comparing, since the gap between the two lists is often the real conversation. The goal in session is not to settle who is right but to agree on a shared, current list to work from. End with one or two tasks either partner is willing to shift, rather than renegotiating everything at once.

fields.label: Partner A: tasks I believe I mostly handle

title: Weekly State of the Union Guide
summary: A structured 20-minute weekly check-in guide covering what went well and what needs attention.
goal: Give a couple a standing time and structure to talk before small issues pile up.
body_md: Set a recurring time rather than waiting for a natural opening, since couples who wait tend to only talk during conflict. Open with appreciations before moving to concerns, and close by naming one thing to try differently before the next check-in. The structure matters more than any single week’s content; it is the habit that keeps small issues from becoming a backlog.

fields.label: What went well between us this week
What felt off or needs attention
Anything logistical to plan for next week
One thing we will try differently

title: Feelings Dial Craft
summary: A paper spinner a child decorates and turns to show which feeling is biggest right now.
goal: Give a child a quick, low-words way to show an adult how they are feeling.
body_md: The parent helps the child draw and color a face for each feeling word around the dial, then the child practices spinning to whatever feels true right now. A dial gives a child who struggles to find words a way to point instead of speak. Keep it somewhere the child can reach it on their own, and check in on it together at a calm moment first, not only during a hard one.

fields.label: Parent: feeling words we picked together
Child: the face I drew for happy

Child: the face I drew for a feeling I do not have a word for yet

title: Calm-Down Toolbox Build
summary: A small physical box a child fills with objects and pictures that help them calm down.
goal: Give a child a hands-on set of tools they helped choose for calming down.
body_md: Let the child pick and decorate a box, then fill it together with small items like a soft cloth, a breathing card, or a favorite drawing. A tool the child chose themselves gets used far more than one an adult picked alone. The parent’s job is to introduce the box before a meltdown, not during one, so it is familiar when it is needed.

fields.label: Child: what I decorated my box with
Child: the things I put inside and why

title: Strength Shield Craft
summary: A paper shield a child decorates with pictures of their own strengths and people who help them.
goal: Give a child a visual reminder of their own strengths and support.
body_md: Divide the shield into sections for something the child is good at, something they are proud of, and someone who helps them, and let them draw rather than write if that is easier. The parent’s role is to ask open questions and add ideas the child might not think of alone, not to fill in the answers. Hang the finished shield somewhere the child sees it often.

A person who helps me

title: Parent Coaching Sheet: Descriptive Praise
summary: A coaching sheet teaching a parent to praise the specific behavior they want to see more of.
goal: Help a parent give praise specific enough for a child to know exactly what to repeat.
duration: 15 minutes to review, then daily practice
body_md: Contrast a vague praise like "good job" with a descriptive one that names the exact behavior, such as noting that the child put their shoes away without being asked. Descriptive praise tells a child precisely what worked, so it is more likely to happen again. Ask the parent to try it three times a day and bring back what they noticed about their child’s response.

title: Morning Launch Pad Chart
summary: A picture chart of the morning routine a child checks off as each step is finished.
goal: Reduce morning conflict by making the routine visible and predictable.
duration: 20 minutes to build, then daily use
body_md: Draw or print a small picture for each step, like getting dressed or eating breakfast, and let the child help order them and add stickers as they finish each one. A chart the child helped make holds their attention longer than one handed to them finished. Keep the list short enough to actually finish before it becomes another source of pressure.

fields.label: Child: the steps in my morning, in order
Child: which step is hardest for me
Parent: what usually slows the morning down

title: Two Truths and a Feeling
summary: A group icebreaker where each player shares two true facts and one true feeling for the group to guess apart.
goal: Warm a group up while normalizing naming feelings out loud.
body_md: Each player shares three statements: two ordinary facts and one honest feeling, and the group guesses which is the feeling. Model the first round yourself so the tone stays light rather than turning into a confession. Debrief by asking what it was like to say a real feeling out loud in a group, since that is the actual point of the game.

What the group guessed

title: Coping Skills Scavenger Hunt
summary: A group game where teams race to name a coping skill fitting each card drawn from a deck.
goal: Make recalling coping skills quick and playful instead of effortful.
body_md: Draw cards naming a feeling or situation and have teams race to name a coping skill that fits, awarding points for speed and a bonus for a skill no other team named. The pace keeps it playful and builds real recall speed for later. Debrief by asking which skills came to mind fastest and which ones the group forgot until it was said aloud.

fields.label: A card and the skill my team named
A skill another team named that I want to remember
The skill that came to mind fastest for me

title: Values Marketplace Game
summary: A group game where players "spend" a limited budget of tokens across cards naming different values.
goal: Make a values discussion concrete by forcing real trade-offs.
body_md: Give each player a small, equal budget of tokens and a spread of cards naming values like family, achievement, or rest, then have them spend the budget across the cards that matter most to them. The forced scarcity is the point: it surfaces real priorities faster than an open-ended list would. Debrief by comparing where the group spent similarly and where they differed.

fields.label: Where I spent most of my tokens
A value I wanted to spend on but ran out of tokens for
Where my spending surprised me

title: Freeze and Think Game
summary: A movement game where children freeze on a cue and name one thought before moving again.
goal: Build a child’s habit of pausing to notice a thought before reacting.
body_md: Children move around freely until a freeze cue, at which point each names one thought or feeling out loud before play resumes. The freeze itself is the skill being practiced: a brief pause between impulse and action. Keep the pace fun rather than serious, and have the parent or group leader play too, so it does not feel like a test.

fields.label: A thought I named during a freeze
How it felt to pause before moving again
A thought someone else named that I liked

title: Story Cubes Reframe Game
summary: A dice game where players build a fresh interpretation of a tricky situation using rolled picture cubes.
goal: Practice generating alternative interpretations in a low-stakes, playful format.
body_md: Each player rolls a set of picture cubes and has to build a plausible, more balanced interpretation of a shared tricky scenario using the images they rolled. The randomness forces flexible thinking rather than the same well-worn explanation. Debrief by asking which reframe felt most believable and why, tying it back to the client’s own thinking patterns.

fields.label: The scenario the group used
The images I rolled
The reframe I built from them
Which reframe from the group felt most believable

title: Support Network Map
summary: A worksheet mapping who a client can turn to for practical help, comfort, or distraction.
goal: Help the client see and strengthen the support they already have.
body_md: Sort people the client already knows into practical help, comfort, and distraction, without pressure to fill every category. A thin map is useful information, not a failure; it points to where the client might want to build a new connection. Keep the finished map somewhere easy to find on a hard day.

fields.label: Who I can call for practical help
Who I can call just to feel less alone
Who helps me think about something else for a while

title: Hypervigilance Scan Log
summary: A short log noticing moments of scanning for danger and what followed each one.
goal: Help the client see hypervigilance as a pattern they can name, not a personal flaw.
body_md: Ask the client to note a few moments a day when they caught themselves scanning a room or a person for danger, along with what setting they were in. Reviewed together, the log usually reveals a pattern of places or situations rather than randomness. Frame the scanning as a system that learned to protect them and is now firing more often than the present moment needs.

title: Values Beyond the Alarm Practice
summary: An exercise linking one small values-based action to a day when the alarm system feels loud.
goal: Help the client take a small step toward what matters even while on edge.
body_md: Ask what matters to the client today, then ask for one small action in that direction that is doable even with the alarm system running high. The point is not to wait for calm before living; it is choosing a value-aligned step alongside whatever the body is doing. Keep the step small enough that it does not become one more thing to fail at.

fields.label: What matters to me today
How loud my alarm system feels right now (0-10)

title: Self-Soothing Senses Kit Card
summary: A card listing one self-soothing option for each of the five senses, chosen in session.
goal: Give the client fast, sensory options for calming an activated body.
duration: 15 minutes to build, then in the moment
body_md: Build the card together, one soothing option per sense, using things the client actually likes rather than a generic list. A scent, a texture, a sound, a taste, and something pleasant to look at give the body several doors back to calm. Keep the items or a note of where to find them close at hand, and revisit the card if an option stops working.

fields.label: Sight: something calming to look at
Sound: something calming to hear
Smell: something calming to smell

title: Supporting Without Fixing Conversation
summary: A guided conversation helping partners talk about what support looks like without either partner trying to fix the other.
goal: Give a couple shared language for support that does not slide into pressure or rescue.
body_md: Ask each partner what support has actually helped in the past and what has felt like pressure, even when well meant. Many partners default to problem-solving because it feels useful, when what is wanted is presence. Close by naming one or two concrete things the supporting partner can do next time that are not about fixing anything.

Partner A: support that has felt like pressure
Partner B: support that has helped me

title: Worry Jar Craft
summary: A decorated jar where a child places written or drawn worries at a set time each day.
goal: Give a child a physical place to put a worry down instead of carrying it all day.
duration: 20 minutes to build, then daily use
body_md: The child decorates a jar and, at a set time each evening, writes or draws one worry on a slip and drops it in. The parent sets the time and sits nearby without solving the worry on the spot; the jar’s job is to hold it until later, not to make it disappear. Look through the jar together once a week and notice which worries are still around and which ones faded.

title: Anxiety Ladder Board Game
summary: A homemade board game where landing on a square names a small step up the client’s own anxiety ladder.
goal: Make reviewing an exposure hierarchy playful instead of dreaded.
body_md: Build a simple path board with squares drawn from the client’s own hierarchy of feared situations, from easiest to hardest, and take turns rolling to move and reading the square aloud. Landing on a square is a chance to rate confidence for that step, not to actually do it in the moment. Debrief by asking which squares felt easier to look at than expected.

title: Safety Behavior Drop List
summary: A worksheet listing the small habits a client uses to feel safer and rating which ones to try dropping first.
goal: Help the client see which safety behaviors are quietly keeping their anxiety alive.
body_md: List habits like checking a phone repeatedly, over-preparing, or avoiding eye contact, and rate each on how much relief it gives against how much it keeps the anxiety fed. A safety behavior can look helpful while quietly confirming that danger was real all along. Pick the lowest-stakes one to drop first, and plan what to do instead when the urge to use it shows up.

title: Catastrophizing Chain Breaker
summary: A worksheet that walks a catastrophic thought chain back to its first, most believable link.
goal: Show the client where a worry spiral leaves realistic ground.
body_md: Write out the full chain from "what if" to worst case, then go back and rate how believable each link is on its own, not as part of the chain. Most chains lose credibility fast after the first one or two steps, which is easy to miss while caught up in the spiral. Use the point where believability drops as the new, more realistic stopping point.

title: Anxious Thoughts Backseat Driver Practice
summary: A metaphor practice picturing anxious thoughts as a backseat passenger giving directions the client no longer has to follow.
goal: Give the client a felt sense of driving their own life alongside a loud anxious voice.
body_md: Walk through the metaphor of anxiety as a backseat passenger who can talk as much as it wants but does not hold the wheel. Ask the client to picture a recent moment anxiety tried to grab the wheel and what it would have looked like to keep driving anyway. This is a rehearsal for noticing the difference between the passenger’s voice and the client’s own choices.

title: Opposite Action for Low Mood Card
summary: A pocket card applying opposite action to the urge to withdraw when mood is low.
goal: Give the client a structured way to act against a withdrawal urge that does not fit the moment.
duration: 15 minutes to learn, then in the moment
body_md: Name the urge to withdraw, check whether it fits the actual facts of the situation, and plan the opposite action, done fully rather than halfway. This is not about forcing cheer; it is choosing engaged behavior even while the mood itself has not shifted yet. Start with a small, low-stakes version before asking the client to try it somewhere that matters more.

fields.label: The urge to withdraw I am noticing
Does the urge fit the facts of the situation?

title: Supporting a Low Mood Without Fixing It Conversation
summary: A guided conversation for partners on what actually helps versus what adds pressure when one partner’s mood is low.
goal: Give a couple language for support that does not turn into pressure to feel better.
body_md: Ask the partner with low mood what has helped in the past and what has felt like pressure, and ask the supporting partner what has felt hardest to know how to do. It is common for a well-meaning partner to push for solutions or cheerfulness when presence would help more. Close with one or two specific things the supporting partner can offer without expecting an immediate change in mood.

fields.label: What has actually helped me when my mood is low
What has felt like pressure, even if well meant
What feels hardest for me as the supporting partner
One thing we agree to try next time

title: Feelings Under the Weather Chart
summary: A weather-themed chart a child fills in daily to show whether today feels sunny, cloudy, or stormy inside.
goal: Give a child a simple, visual way to show low mood without needing the right words.
body_md: The child colors in a weather symbol each day for how they feel inside, and the parent asks one gentle open question about whatever symbol was picked rather than pushing for detail. A string of cloudy or stormy days is useful information for the parent and clinician to notice together, not something to fix in the moment. Keep the chart low pressure and easy to skip a day without consequence.

Child: one thing that happened today

title: Low Mood Scavenger Hunt
summary: A group game where players hunt for small, doable mood-lifting actions hidden around a list of categories.
goal: Make generating behavioral activation ideas playful and collaborative.
body_md: Give the group categories like movement, connection, sunlight, and a small accomplishment, and have players race to name or find something in each that takes five minutes or less. The short time limit keeps the ideas realistic rather than aspirational. Debrief by asking which ideas from the hunt someone might actually try this week.

title: Morning Anchor Routine Sheet
summary: A short, fixed sequence of two or three morning actions the client commits to on the hardest days.
goal: Give the client a minimum viable morning that does not depend on motivation.
body_md: Pick two or three small, concrete actions the client can do even on a low day, like opening the curtains, drinking water, and getting out of bed by a set time. The anchor routine is deliberately small so it stays doable when motivation is at its lowest; anything beyond it is a bonus, not a requirement. Review which days the anchor held and which days it slipped, without treating a slip as failure.

title: Working Memory Workaround Log
summary: A log tracking which external memory tools actually got used this week and which got forgotten.
goal: Help the client find which reminder systems work for them instead of assuming willpower will.
body_md: Have the client try two or three external memory tools, like a visible list, phone alarms, or sticky notes in a specific spot, and log which ones actually got checked. The goal is finding a workaround that fits the client’s life, not proving they should simply remember better. Keep whichever tool got used most, even if it seems unusually simple.

title: Present Task Anchor Practice
summary: A brief practice for noticing when attention has drifted and returning to the task at hand without self-criticism.
goal: Build the client’s skill of returning to a task gently, over and over, instead of giving up after one drift.
body_md: Teach the client to notice a drift, name it lightly, and return to the task without adding a layer of self-criticism on top. Attention drifting is expected, not a sign of failure, and the skill being built is the return, not staying perfectly focused. Practice with a short, low-stakes task before applying it to something the client is avoiding.

title: Impulse Pause Card
summary: A wallet card walking through a brief pause before acting on an impulsive urge.
goal: Give the client a repeatable structure for creating a few seconds of space before acting.
duration: 10 minutes to learn, then in the moment
body_md: Practice the pause on a low-stakes impulse in session first: notice the urge, take one slow breath, and ask what the client actually wants a minute from now versus right now. A few seconds of space is often enough to change what happens next without requiring the urge to disappear. Track which situations the pause worked in and which ones still need more practice.

title: Reminder System Agreement for Partners
summary: A guided conversation for a couple to agree on reminder systems that feel supportive rather than like nagging.
goal: Reduce reminder-related conflict by agreeing on the method up front.
body_md: Ask the partner with ADHD which kinds of reminders actually help and which feel like nagging, and ask the other partner what feels sustainable to keep offering. A shared, agreed system, like a written list checked once a day rather than repeated spoken reminders, tends to reduce friction on both sides. Revisit the agreement after a couple of weeks rather than assuming it will hold forever.

title: Fidget and Focus Toolkit Build
summary: A small kit of fidget and sensory tools a child helps choose to support focus during quiet tasks.
goal: Give a child a hands-on set of tools they helped pick for sitting through a task.
body_md: Let the child test a few fidget or sensory items and pick the ones that actually help rather than distract, then decorate a small pouch to keep them in. A tool the child chose gets used more than one an adult picked alone. The parent’s job is introducing the kit before homework time starts, so it is a familiar routine and not a last-minute fix.

title: Urge Timer Challenge Game
summary: A group game where players practice riding out a timed urge together while naming what they notice.
goal: Give a group practice tolerating an urge for a set time without acting on it.
body_md: Set a short timer and have each player picture a mild urge from their own experience, then narrate out loud what they notice in their body as the group waits it out together. Practicing with a mild, willing example builds the skill before it is needed for something harder. Debrief by asking what changed in the urge between the start of the timer and the end.

title: Values and Substance Use Conflict Map
summary: A worksheet mapping where substance use and the client’s own stated values pull in different directions.
goal: Help the client see the conflict between substance use and what actually matters to them, in their own words.
body_md: List the client’s top values, then ask honestly where substance use supports each one and where it works against it. The map is meant to build the client’s own case, not to argue one for them; ambivalence stated in the client’s own words moves more than a clinician’s argument would. Keep the tone curious rather than confrontational throughout.

title: Permission-Giving Thoughts Log
summary: A log catching the specific thought that gives permission to act on an urge in the moment.
goal: Help the client spot the exact thought that opens the door, so it can be caught earlier next time.
body_md: Ask the client to write down the thought that showed up right before acting on an urge, such as telling themselves it is just this once or that they have earned it. These permission-giving thoughts often go unnoticed because they feel reasonable in the moment. Reviewing the log together builds the client’s ability to catch the thought earlier, while there is still room to choose differently.

title: Willing Hands Urge Practice
summary: A brief practice for holding an urge with open, willing hands instead of fighting or acting on it.
goal: Give the client a physical posture that supports willingness during a strong urge.
body_md: Have the client physically open their hands, palms up, while describing the urge out loud, noticing the pull to either grip it tightly or push it away. Neither fighting the urge nor giving in to it is the goal; the practice is letting it be present without acting on it. Rehearse it with a mild urge before asking the client to use it somewhere harder.

title: Emotion Regulation for Urges Card
summary: A card connecting the specific emotion under an urge to a matching regulation skill.
goal: Help the client treat urges as messages from an emotion, not just a craving to fight.
duration: 15 minutes to build, then in the moment
body_md: Ask the client what emotion usually sits underneath their strongest urges, like loneliness, boredom, or shame, and match each one to a regulation skill that actually addresses it. An urge treated only as a craving misses the emotional signal driving it. Keep the card specific to the client’s own patterns rather than a generic list.

fields.label: The emotion most often under my urges
A skill that addresses that emotion directly

title: Fair Fighting Ground Rules Agreement
summary: A shared agreement both partners sign on how they want to handle conflict when anger rises.
goal: Give a couple ground rules agreed in advance, before the next conflict starts.
body_md: Draft rules together while calm, such as no name-calling, taking a break if a voice rises, and returning to finish the conversation later. Rules made together tend to stick better than rules imposed by one partner on the other. Post the finished agreement somewhere visible and revisit it after it has been tested by a real disagreement.

fields.label: A rule we both agree to
Our signal for calling a break
How long our break will be
How we will return to finish the conversation

title: Anger Weather Report Craft
summary: A weather-themed craft a child builds to show how their anger moves from a light breeze to a storm.
goal: Give a child a visual way to notice anger building before it peaks.
body_md: Build a simple weather scale together, from a calm sunny day to a storm, and ask the child to describe what their body feels like at each stage. The parent’s role is helping the child notice the early stages, like a breeze picking up, since those are the moments a skill can still help. Practice checking the weather report at a calm moment before trying it during an actual upset.

fields.label: What my body feels like on a calm day
What my body feels like when the breeze picks up
What my body feels like in a storm

title: Anger Triggers Relay Game
summary: A relay game where teams race to match anger triggers to a matching cooling skill.
goal: Build quick recall of cooling skills that fit specific triggers.
body_md: Set up two stations with trigger cards and skill cards, and have teams race to run a trigger card to its matching skill card before time runs out. The physical movement and time pressure make the matching stick better than a static worksheet. Debrief by asking which matches were obvious and which ones took more thought.

fields.label: A trigger and the skill my team matched to it

title: Early Warning Signs Ladder
summary: A ladder from calm to full anger, with the client’s own body and thought signs at each rung.
goal: Help the client catch anger earlier, while more options are still available.
body_md: Build the ladder from the client’s own recent experiences, naming the body sensations and thoughts at each rung from calm to full anger. Most clients can describe the top rung easily but struggle to name the early ones, which is exactly where the useful work happens. Once named, pick one skill to try at an early rung this week.

title: Unfair Rules Rewrite Sheet
summary: A worksheet identifying the rigid rules underneath an anger reaction and testing how fair they really are.
goal: Help the client loosen the rigid rules that turn small frustrations into big reactions.
body_md: Write down the unspoken rule behind a recent angry reaction, such as believing people should always be on time, and test how realistic and fair that rule actually is across different situations. Rigid rules about how others should behave tend to generate frequent, disproportionate anger. Rewrite the rule into something more flexible that still reflects what the client cares about.

title: Uncertainty Willingness Ladder
summary: A ladder of situations rated by how much uncertainty the client is willing to sit with, without checking or ritual.
goal: Build the client’s willingness to tolerate not knowing, one step at a time.
body_md: List situations that trigger the urge for certainty, from mild to intense, and rate the client’s current willingness to sit with each without resolving it. The ladder is about willingness, not proof of safety; the client is not being asked to believe nothing bad will happen, only to make room for not knowing. Pick a low rung to practice with before the next session.

title: Riding Out the Urge to Ritualize Card
summary: A pocket card walking through riding out the urge to complete a ritual without acting on it.
goal: Give the client a structure for delaying and observing an urge to ritualize.
duration: 15 minutes to learn, then in the moment
body_md: Practice the sequence in session: name the urge, rate its intensity, set a short delay, and notice what happens to the urge during the delay without judging the outcome. The urge to ritualize tends to rise and fall on its own if given time, which is easy to forget mid-urge. Build the delay up gradually rather than expecting a long one on the first try.

title: Reducing Reassurance Together Conversation
summary: A guided conversation helping a couple agree on a plan for reducing reassurance-seeking together.
goal: Give a couple a shared, gradual plan for stepping back from reassurance cycles.
body_md: Ask both partners to name the current reassurance patterns and how each one feels giving or asking for it. A partner who gives reassurance is often trying to help and may not realize it is keeping the cycle going; naming this together reduces blame on either side. Agree on one small, gradual step to reduce the pattern, with a plan for how the supporting partner can respond instead.

title: Worry Bug Talk-Back Craft
summary: A craft where a child builds a "worry bug" character to represent unwanted sticky thoughts, then practices talking back.
goal: Give a child a playful way to separate themselves from an unwanted thought.
body_md: Have the child build or draw a worry bug and give it a name and a silly voice, then practice a few things to say back to it when it shows up. Externalizing the thought as a character makes it something to argue with rather than something that defines the child. The parent’s job is playing along and helping the child notice when the bug is talking, without dismissing how real it feels.

fields.label: My worry bug’s name and what it looks like

title: Delay and Distract Board Game
summary: A board game where landing on a square means practicing a short delay before responding to a pretend urge.
goal: Practice the skill of delaying a response in a low-stakes, playful format.
body_md: Players draw cards describing a mild pretend urge and must wait out a short timer before their next turn, narrating what they notice while they wait. The playful pressure of waiting for a turn mirrors the real skill of tolerating a delay. Debrief by asking which waits felt easy and which felt harder, and why.

title: Panic Symptom Fact Sheet
summary: A worksheet pairing each panic sensation with a plain explanation of what is happening in the body.
goal: Reduce the fear of panic sensations by explaining what is actually happening physically.
body_md: List the client’s own panic sensations, like a racing heart or tight chest, and write a plain, physical explanation next to each one, such as the body preparing extra oxygen and blood flow for a threat it perceives. Naming what is happening in ordinary terms takes away some of the mystery that fuels fear. Keep the sheet somewhere the client can reread it right after a panic episode.

fields.label: A sensation I notice during panic

title: Worst Case Realistic Case Comparison
summary: A side-by-side comparison of the client’s worst-case panic fear against what has actually happened before.
goal: Use the client’s own history to weigh a catastrophic prediction against the evidence.
body_md: Write the worst-case fear in one column and, in the other, what has actually happened during past panic episodes. Most clients have lived through many panic attacks without the feared outcome occurring, which is easy to lose sight of mid-episode. Use the comparison to build a more realistic prediction to hold onto next time panic starts.

fields.label: My worst-case fear during panic
What has actually happened in past episodes

title: Riding the Panic Wave Practice
summary: A practice imagining panic as a wave that rises and falls on its own, rather than something to escape.
goal: Help the client stop fighting panic and instead make room for it to pass.
body_md: Walk through the image of panic as a wave with a rise, a peak, and a fall, all of which happen whether or not the client fights it. Fighting or escaping a panic wave tends to extend it; staying present with it, uncomfortable as that is, tends to let it pass sooner. Rehearse the image calmly first, then apply it to a recent panic memory.

fields.label: A recent panic wave I remember
