title: Slow Exhale Reset Card
summary: A pocket card walking through a slow-exhale breathing pattern for calming panic’s physical intensity.
goal: Give the client a fast, physiology-based option for the peak of a panic episode.
body_md: Practice a breathing pattern with a longer exhale than inhale, since a long exhale signals the body’s calming system directly. Rehearse it calm first so the pattern is familiar before the client needs it during panic. Track how many rounds it usually takes before the intensity starts to ease.

fields.label: My breath count in and out
How intense the panic felt before (0-10)
How many rounds I did
How intense it felt after

title: What Helps During a Panic Attack Conversation
summary: A guided conversation for a couple to plan what the supporting partner should and should not do during a panic attack.
goal: Give a couple a clear, agreed plan instead of guessing in the moment.
body_md: Ask the partner who experiences panic exactly what has helped in the past, like a certain phrase, quiet presence, or a breathing cue, and what has made it worse, like rapid questions or urging them to calm down. Agree on a short, specific plan the supporting partner can follow instead of improvising under pressure. Revisit the plan after it has been used for real.

fields.label: What actually helps me during a panic attack
What makes it worse
What the supporting partner will do
What the supporting partner will avoid doing

title: Choices Chart Craft
summary: A craft chart offering a child two acceptable choices for common daily tasks, built together with a parent.
goal: Give a child a sense of control within limits a parent sets.
body_md: For a few recurring tasks, the parent and child draw two acceptable options and let the child pick, like choosing which shirt to wear or which chore to do first. Offering a real choice between two things a parent can live with reduces power struggles without giving up the boundary. Keep the chart to a few tasks at first rather than trying to cover the whole day.

fields.label: Parent: the tasks we picked for the chart
Parent: the two choices for each task
Child: which choices I picked this week
Parent: what changed about our mornings or routines

title: Family Feelings Charades
summary: A family game where players act out a feeling for others to guess, then share a time they felt it.
goal: Build a family’s shared vocabulary for naming feelings out loud.
body_md: Each player draws a feeling word and acts it out without speaking while the rest of the family guesses, then the player shares one real moment they felt that way. Acting it out first makes the sharing that follows feel lighter and less put-on-the-spot. Parents modeling their own examples helps children feel it is safe to share theirs too.

fields.label: The feeling I acted out
A time I actually felt that way
A feeling someone else shared that surprised me
What it was like to share a real moment with the family

title: Consistency Tracker for Consequences
summary: A weekly tracker checking whether a chosen consequence was followed through the same way each time.
goal: Help a parent see where inconsistency is undermining an otherwise reasonable rule.
body_md: For one agreed rule and consequence, the parent logs each day whether it held or slipped, and what made it harder to follow through on the slipped days. Most inconsistency comes from fatigue or a public setting, not from the rule being wrong, which is useful to separate out. Use the pattern to plan for the specific moments that make follow-through hardest.

fields.label: The rule and consequence we are tracking
Day by day: held or slipped
What made the slipped days harder
What would make follow-through easier next time

title: Parent Guilt Thought Check
summary: A worksheet testing a guilty parenting thought against what the parent would actually tell a friend.
goal: Help a parent separate a guilty thought from a fair assessment of their parenting.
body_md: Write the guilty thought exactly as it occurs, then ask what the parent would say to a close friend who described the same situation about their own child. Parents are often far harsher with themselves than they would ever be with someone else, and the gap is worth naming directly. Use the friend’s-eye view to write a fairer version of the original thought.

fields.label: The guilty thought
What I would tell a friend in the same situation

title: Parenting Values Compass
summary: A compass exercise naming what kind of parent the client wants to be, separate from any single hard moment.
goal: Give a parent a values-based anchor to return to when a day has gone badly.
body_md: Ask the client to describe the kind of parent they want to be in a few concrete words, then compare a recent hard day against that direction without treating one bad moment as proof of failure. A single yelling match does not erase the direction a parent is generally moving in. Use the compass to choose one small repair or next step rather than a full self-assessment.

fields.label: The kind of parent I want to be, in my own words
A recent moment that felt far from that
A recent moment that felt close to it
One small step back toward my direction

title: Emotional Wave Riding Card for New Parents
summary: A pocket card for riding out sudden waves of overwhelm or tearfulness common in the early postpartum weeks.
goal: Give a new parent a fast way to ride out an intense wave without judging it.
duration: 10 minutes to learn, then in the moment
body_md: Teach the client to name the wave, take a few slow breaths, and remind themselves the wave will pass, without pressure to feel differently right away. Sudden waves of overwhelm are common in early parenthood, and knowing they pass on their own reduces the fear that they will not. Keep the card short enough to glance at one-handed while holding a baby.

fields.label: The wave I noticed today

title: Division of Night Wakings Conversation
summary: A guided conversation for a couple to agree on a fair, realistic plan for splitting overnight care.
goal: Reduce resentment by making the overnight plan explicit instead of assumed.
body_md: Ask each partner what the current overnight pattern actually looks like and how it feels, since one partner’s sense of who is doing what often differs sharply from the other’s. Build a concrete plan for the coming weeks, including how it will flex around work schedules or feeding method. Agree to revisit the plan again soon rather than treating it as fixed.

title: Big Sibling Feelings Kit Craft
summary: A craft kit helping an older sibling name and express feelings about a new baby in the house.
goal: Give an older sibling a way to express mixed feelings about a new baby without needing perfect words.
body_md: Build a small kit with a feelings chart and a "big sibling job card" the child helps design, so they have both a way to name hard feelings and a concrete role with the baby. Mixed feelings, including jealousy, are ordinary and worth making room for rather than correcting. The parent’s job is checking in with the kit regularly, not just when the child is visibly upset.

title: New Parent Circle Check-In Game
summary: A group check-in game for a new parent support circle, passing a token while sharing one honest line about the week.
goal: Warm up a new parent group and normalize honest sharing early in the session.
body_md: Pass a small object around the circle, and whoever holds it shares one honest line about their week, good, hard, or both, before passing it on. The structure gives everyone a turn without putting anyone on the spot to say more than they want. Close by asking what it was like to hear other parents say something similarly honest.

title: Realistic Fourth Trimester Expectations Sheet
summary: A worksheet comparing the expectations a new parent had for early parenthood against what has actually happened.
goal: Reduce shame by naming the gap between expected and actual early parenthood out loud.
body_md: List what the client expected the early weeks to feel like, then what has actually happened, without judging either column. Most new parents carry expectations shaped by curated images rather than the realities of recovery, feeding, and sleep. Use the gap to identify one expectation worth letting go of this week.

title: Self-Talk Swap Card
summary: A pocket card pairing the client’s harshest self-talk phrases with a swap they can actually believe.
goal: Give the client a fast, believable alternative to reach for instead of a harsh automatic phrase.
body_md: List the client’s most common harsh phrases, then work together to find a swap that is kinder but still believable rather than a forced positive. A swap that feels fake gets dismissed the moment it is needed; one the client can actually stand behind gets used. Practice saying a few swaps out loud before the client leaves.

title: Self-Compassion Break for Self-Esteem
summary: A short three-part practice pairing a hard self-esteem moment with kindness rather than argument.
goal: Give the client a way to respond to a self-esteem hit with kindness instead of a counterattack.
body_md: Walk through three steps: naming that this is a hard moment, remembering that struggling with self-worth is common and not unique to the client, and offering themselves a kind phrase. This is a practice of responding differently to the moment, not a debate about whether the harsh thought is true. Rehearse it with a mild example before asking the client to use it somewhere harder.

title: Self-Respect Effectiveness Check
summary: A quick check weighing whether a planned response protects the client’s self-respect as well as the outcome.
goal: Add self-respect as a deliberate factor in how the client decides to respond to a situation.
body_md: Before a planned conversation or decision, ask the client to check the response against three things: does it get the outcome wanted, does it protect the relationship, and does it keep their own self-respect. Clients who chronically under-value themselves often skip the third question entirely. Adjust the planned response until all three hold up reasonably well.

title: Building Each Other Up Conversation
summary: A guided conversation where partners share how the other’s words affect their self-esteem, for better or worse.
goal: Help a couple see the real weight their words carry for each other’s self-esteem.
body_md: Ask each partner to name a phrase or moment that genuinely lifted their self-esteem and one that landed harder than the other partner likely intended. Partners often underestimate how much casual comments shape each other’s self-view over time. Close by naming one thing each partner will try to say more often.

title: My Superpowers Poster Craft
summary: A poster a child decorates naming their own "superpowers," drawn from real strengths a parent points out too.
goal: Give a child a visible, ongoing reminder of their own strengths.
body_md: The child draws themselves as a superhero and labels their real strengths as superpowers, with the parent adding one or two the child might not think to include. Naming a strength as a power the child already has, rather than something to earn, supports a steadier sense of self-worth. Hang the poster somewhere visible and add to it as new strengths show up.

goal: Give the client low-stakes practice starting and holding a short conversation.
body_md: Players draw a starter question and pair up for a short, timed exchange before rotating partners. The structure removes the hardest part, deciding what to say first, so the focus shifts to practicing the exchange itself. Debrief by asking which starters felt easiest and what the client noticed in their body during and after each round.

goal: Give the client and clinician a shared plan for gradually approaching feared social situations.
body_md: List a range of social situations, from a brief hallway greeting to speaking up in a full meeting, and rate current confidence for each. Build the ladder from the client’s real life rather than a generic list, so the rungs feel relevant. Agree on the next rung to attempt before the following session, and note what support might help.

title: Spotlight Effect Reality Check
summary: A worksheet testing the belief that others noticed a social mistake as much as the client thinks they did.
goal: Weaken the belief that everyone is watching and judging as closely as it feels.
body_md: Describe a recent moment the client felt embarrassed, then estimate how much others actually noticed against how much it felt like they noticed. People generally notice and remember others’ small slips far less than the person experiencing them assumes, which the client can test with their own memory of others’ mistakes. Use the gap to build a more realistic estimate for next time.

title: Willing to Be Awkward Practice
summary: A practice building willingness to feel awkward on purpose, in service of connecting with others.
goal: Reduce the grip of needing to feel comfortable before the client will engage socially.
body_md: Ask the client to name a small social action they have been avoiding until it feels comfortable, and reframe the goal as being willing to feel awkward while doing it anyway. goal: Give the client a structured way to follow through on a social plan despite the urge to cancel.
duration: 15 minutes to learn, then in the moment
body_md: Check whether the urge to cancel fits the actual facts of the situation, then plan the opposite action of showing up, done fully rather than with an early exit already planned. Canceling brings short-term relief but tends to strengthen the avoidance pattern over time. Start with a lower-stakes plan before applying it to something that matters more.

goal: Reduce conflict between partners who grieve at different paces or in different ways.

Partners grieving the same loss often grieve differently, and mismatched styles can read as one partner not caring when that is not what is happening. Close with one specific thing each partner can offer the other going forward.

goal: Give a child a hands-on way to hold onto memories of someone they lost.
body_md: The child decorates a jar and, over time, adds slips with a memory, a favorite thing about the person, or a question they wish they could ask. The parent’s role is helping without steering, since the memories that matter to the child may differ from what an adult expects. goal: Give a grief group a low-pressure, structured way to share without needing to say everything.
body_md: Go around the circle with each person sharing one memory, word, or feeling connected to their loss, with an easy pass option for anyone not ready. The round structure means no one has to carry the conversation alone, and the pass option keeps participation genuinely optional. Close by asking what it was like to hear others share alongside their own.

goal: Help the client see grief waves as a pattern rather than a sign that healing is not happening.

Waves are a normal part of grief and often connect to specific triggers, like a song, a date, or a smell, which can be named once tracked. Reviewing the log together helps the client anticipate rather than be blindsided by predictable waves.

title: Guilt and Responsibility Sorting Sheet

goal: Help the client separate real responsibility from guilt that does not hold up under examination.

Grief often produces guilt about things no one could have controlled or known, and separating the two categories does not erase the guilt but gives it somewhere honest to sit. Revisit the sheet over several sessions rather than expecting it to resolve in one.

goal: Reduce the delay between a conflict and a repair attempt.

title: Validation Practice Card for Partners

title: Grounding Object Inventory
summary: A worksheet listing small objects the client can carry that help them feel grounded and present.
goal: Give the client a concrete, portable set of grounding supports chosen in session.
body_md: List a few small objects, like a textured stone, a piece of jewelry, or a scented item, that help the client feel present and safe, and note where each one will be kept. Choosing the objects together in a calm moment means they are ready before they are needed. Revisit the list occasionally, since what grounds a client can change over time.

title: Self-Blame Thought Check
summary: A worksheet gently testing a self-blame thought against what the client would say to someone else in their position.
goal: Help the client loosen a self-blame thought without needing to revisit what happened in detail.
body_md: Write the self-blame thought exactly as it occurs, then ask what the client would say to a friend who described feeling the same way. This works without asking the client to recount events; the focus stays on the thought itself and how it is being applied to them versus how it would be applied to someone else. Use the comparison to build a fairer version of the thought to return to.

title: Safe Enough Right Now Practice
summary: A brief grounding practice checking the difference between present-moment safety and past danger.
goal: Help the client anchor in present-moment safety without needing to revisit the past in detail.
body_md: Guide the client through naming where they are right now, who is nearby, and what tells them this moment is different from a remembered one, without asking them to describe the remembered moment itself. The practice stays entirely in the present; it is a check on now, not a reprocessing of then. Keep sessions short and let the client set the pace for how much they want to do.

title: Distress Tolerance Menu for Hard Moments
summary: A menu of distress tolerance skills the client rates for how well each one has worked for them personally.
goal: Give the client a personalized, ranked menu of skills to reach for in a hard moment.
body_md: Go through a range of distress tolerance skills, from temperature change to paced breathing to a self-soothing item, and have the client rate how well each has worked for them in the past. A personalized, ranked menu is faster to use under stress than a generic list. Keep the menu short enough to scan quickly and update it as new skills prove useful.

title: Supporting Without Pressuring Conversation
summary: A guided conversation for partners on offering support at whatever pace feels safe, without pressure to share more.
goal: Give a couple language for support that respects pacing and does not push for detail.
body_md: Ask the partner who experienced the harm what kind of support has felt safe and what has felt like pressure, and ask the supporting partner what has felt hardest about not knowing how to help. Support here means presence and patience, not encouraging the other partner to share more than they are ready to. Close with one or two specific things the supporting partner can offer that do not depend on hearing more detail.

title: Calm Down Cards Deck Craft
summary: A homemade deck of cards a child decorates, each one showing a different coping skill to try.
goal: Give a child a physical deck of coping options they helped make and can pick from freely.
body_md: The child draws a picture for each coping skill on its own card, like blowing bubbles, squeezing a pillow, or counting backward, and decorates a small box to keep the deck in. Letting the child pick a card themselves when upset gives them a sense of choice that a single fixed instruction does not. The parent’s role is offering the deck early, before things escalate, rather than in the middle of a meltdown.

title: Coping Skills Hot Potato
summary: A group circle game where players pass an object and name a coping skill before passing it on.
goal: Build fast, playful recall of a range of coping skills.
body_md: Players pass an object around the circle to music or a countdown, and whoever holds it when the count stops names a coping skill before play continues. The quick pace keeps recall fast and light rather than effortful. Debrief by listing every skill the group named and circling any the client wants to remember.

goal: Help the client see which categories of coping they lean on and which are underused.
body_md: List coping skills the client already uses under categories like distraction, soothing, expression, and connection, then notice which categories are full and which are nearly empty. goal: Give the client brief, memorized phrases to interrupt a spiral before it builds.
body_md: Write a handful of short phrases the client actually believes, like reminding themselves this feeling will pass or that they have gotten through hard moments before. goal: Help the client notice the difference between coping that avoids a feeling and coping that makes room for it.

Neither pile is wrong, but a client who relies only on avoidance-based coping may benefit from building the second pile. title: Riding Out Fear Sensations Card
summary: A pocket card for riding out the physical sensations of fear during an exposure step without escaping.
goal: Give the client a way to stay present with fear sensations long enough for them to ease.
duration: 15 minutes to learn, then in the moment
body_md: Practice naming the sensation, rating its intensity, and staying with it for a set stretch of time rather than escaping at the first spike. Fear sensations tend to ease if given time, which is easy to forget in the moment. Build the stretch of time up gradually across exposure steps rather than expecting a long one immediately.

title: Supporting an Exposure Step Conversation
summary: A guided conversation for a couple to agree on how a supporting partner can help during an exposure step without taking over.
goal: Give a couple a clear, agreed role for the supporting partner during exposure practice.
body_md: Ask the partner doing exposure work what kind of presence actually helps, like staying nearby without narrating reassurance, and ask the supporting partner what feels hard about holding back. A supporting partner who steps in too quickly can unintentionally reduce the exposure’s effect. Agree on a specific, limited role the supporting partner will play during the next practice.

goal: Give a child a tangible marker of progress on a fear they are working on.
body_md: After the child completes an agreed small step toward their fear, they design and decorate a badge to mark it, choosing colors and symbols that feel meaningful to them. A physical badge gives a young child something concrete to point to as evidence of their own courage. title: Fear Facts Trivia Game
summary: A trivia game testing what players actually know about a feared object or situation versus what they assume.
goal: Separate real facts about a feared object from assumptions that fuel the fear.
body_md: Ask a mix of true and false questions about a feared object or situation, like how rare a particular danger actually is, and have players guess before revealing the answer. Many phobias are fed by assumptions rather than facts, and a playful quiz format makes correcting those assumptions feel lighter than a lecture. Debrief by asking which facts surprised the group most.

title: Nonjudgmental Body Talk Card
summary: A pocket card practicing describing the body in neutral, factual terms instead of judgmental ones.
goal: Build the client’s ability to notice and describe the body without an automatic judgment attached.
body_md: Practice describing a part of the body in purely factual, nonjudgmental terms, like noting its shape or what it lets the client do, and compare it to the judgmental version that usually comes first. This is a language practice more than a belief change; the skill is catching the judgment and setting it aside, even briefly. Repeat with a few different examples across sessions.

title: Reassurance Seeking About Appearance Conversation
summary: A guided conversation helping a couple find a healthier pattern around appearance-related reassurance seeking.
goal: Reduce a reassurance-seeking cycle around appearance that leaves both partners frustrated.
body_md: Ask the partner seeking reassurance what they are actually hoping to feel, and ask the other partner how the constant reassurance requests affect them over time. Reassurance about appearance tends to give only brief relief before the urge to ask returns, which is worth naming together. Agree on a different response the supporting partner can offer that does not feed the cycle.

title: All Bodies Move Differently Craft
summary: A drawing craft where a child illustrates all the different things bodies in their life can do.
goal: Help a child build an early, function-focused view of bodies rather than an appearance-focused one.
body_md: The child draws people they know doing different things their bodies let them do, like climbing, dancing, hugging, or resting, and the parent asks about what each body in the drawing can do rather than what it looks like. Keeping the conversation focused on ability and action builds a habit of noticing bodies this way early on. Avoid steering the conversation toward appearance, size, or comparison at any point.
